---
title: "Library Guide"
---

This guide explains JAXCMR's data structures, interfaces and conventions:
what each part receives, what it returns and where another part uses it.
It also identifies entry points for supplying compatible functions or
implementations. The [Templates](../templates.qmd) assemble these parts into
complete research procedures.

## How the interfaces connect

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    D["RecallDataset"] --> F["MemorySearchModelFactory"]
    F --> M["MemorySearch"]
    C["Context · Memory · TerminationPolicy"] --> M
    D --> L["LossFn"]
    M -->|event probabilities| L
    M --> S["TrialSimulator"]
    S --> SD["Simulated RecallDataset"]
    D --> A["Recall analyses"]
    SD --> A
    A -. "RecallAnalysisFn callback" .-> L
    L --> O["FittingAlgorithm"]
    O --> R["FitResult"]
    R -->|assigned parameters| S
    R --> E["Evaluation helpers"]
    A --> E
```

A model factory creates a model for an experiment and parameter values.
Likelihood calculations follow recorded responses through that model;
simulation samples new responses. Both observed and simulated datasets
can enter recall analyses. A compatible analysis callback can also supply
the summary used by a behavioral objective. Fitters search parameter values
using a loss and return records for subsequent simulation and evaluation.

Simulation can use hand-chosen parameters without a fit. Analysis can
describe observations without a model. These are connected interfaces,
not a mandatory sequence of steps.

| [Memory Search Models](models.ipynb) | `MemorySearch` and `MemorySearchModelFactory` | Event calculations through `model_factory_cls` in losses and simulation. |

## What a protocol provides

A Python **Protocol** describes the attributes and methods a consumer
expects. A compatible implementation need not inherit from that protocol.
For a callable protocol such as `RecallAnalysisFn`, an ordinary function
with the specified arguments and behavior can be passed directly to its
consumer. The [analysis callback example](analyses.ipynb#recallanalysisfn)
shows this connection using an existing SPC calculation.

Signatures alone are not enough: array dimensions, item coding, parameter
order and JAX-compatible operations also determine whether implementations
work together. Each topic explains these responsibilities alongside the
relevant declaration. Examples illustrate one connection at a time.

`RecallDataset` and `FitResult` are dictionary types, not protocols. They
describe fields and alignment, without being comprehensive runtime
validators. Other conventions, such as template-added provenance or
objective signs expected by comparison helpers, are established by the
procedures that produce and consume the records.

## Configuring a reusable procedure

Template notebooks separate literal settings from the Python objects
constructed from them:

1. A tagged **parameters** cell holds paths, selections, parameter values,
   import names and output locations. Parameterized execution can replace
   these literals for another run.
2. **Setup** imports implementations and constructs factories, masks and
   other derived objects from those settings.
3. The **procedure** produces outputs and retains the effective settings.

Independent executions need separate output locations. Changes to fit
parameters or simulation settings require corresponding new simulation
outputs. The [Templates](../templates.qmd) explain parameterized execution
and provide complete procedures; this guide describes the structures they
connect.

## Using the illustrations

The topic notebooks retain small executed examples using the existing
war-photo-recall observations and supplied fits. Their protocol declarations
are visible; expand a labeled code block to inspect an executable example.
To rerun one, use **Download notebook** and place it beside the shared
`data/` folder from the [Templates downloads](../templates.qmd#download-the-shared-inputs).
The [homepage](../index.ipynb#installation) gives the installation command.
